conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this visit. I’m Maya Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician who works with new mothers. Over the next few minutes we’ll use the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) to check on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. The EPDS is a quick, 10-question screen that helps us spot symptoms of depression or anxiety that can creep up in the postpartum year. Everything you share is confidential, and our only goal is to make sure you feel heard and supported—no judgment, ever.

I’ll ask each question conversationally, and you can answer however feels most comfortable. When we’re done, we’ll look at the results together and talk about next steps that feel right for you. Ready to start?

Thinking about the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. I used to laugh at little things all the time—my husband’s dumb jokes, silly memes—but lately it’s like nothing feels funny. I can still crack a smile if someone really tries, but it feels forced, like I’m pretending to enjoy it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… maybe once or twice this week I sort of chuckled, but it felt flat, like I was going through the motions. Most of the time I’m too tired or worried to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I used to get excited about little plans—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just binge-watching a show—but now it all feels like one more thing I have to get through. I’ll think “that should be fun,” but the feeling doesn’t really come. A couple times I forced myself to go, and I mostly just sat there counting the minutes until I could go home and check on the baby.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… pretty much every day. If she fusses for more than a few minutes, my brain jumps straight to “I’m doing something wrong.” I replay everything—did I eat something that upset her through the milk, did I miss a burp, am I just not soothing her right? Last night she wouldn’t settle for an hour and I sat there crying, telling my husband it must be because I’m a terrible mom. He kept saying she’s just a baby and babies cry, but I still felt like it was my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much all the time. Even when she’s sleeping I’ll suddenly think “what if she stops breathing?” or worry that a tiny rash means something awful. I’ll check her crib camera every few minutes, and if I hear a siren outside I panic that something’s wrong with her. I know it’s probably normal-mom stuff, but it feels constant and I can’t shake it.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yeah… a few times this week. Once I was just folding laundry while she napped and suddenly my heart started racing, I couldn’t catch my breath, and I had this wave of “something terrible is about to happen.” It lasted maybe ten minutes but it felt endless. There wasn’t any real reason—it just hit me out of nowhere.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, the laundry’s piled up, I haven’t eaten a real meal, and I can’t remember if I brushed my teeth. I’ll look at the mess around me and just freeze, thinking, “How does anyone do this?” Some afternoons I end up crying while I rock her because it all feels like too much. I still get through it, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps spinning with everything I might’ve messed up that day or all the scary “what-ifs” about her. Some nights I drift off okay, then jolt awake for her feeding and can’t settle again. I end up staring at the ceiling for hours, feeling this heavy knot in my chest. I’m getting maybe four broken hours a night, if that.
I have felt sad or miserable

A lot of the time. I wake up most mornings feeling this heaviness, like there’s a gray cloud hanging over everything. Even when I’m holding her and she’s smiling, I’ll feel tears behind my eyes for no clear reason. It’s not every single moment—sometimes I’ll have a short stretch that feels okay—but the sadness always creeps back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened three or four times this week. Sometimes it’s because I’m overwhelmed, like when she wouldn’t latch the other night and I just sat there in the rocking chair with tears streaming down. Other times it’s for no real reason at all—I'll just feel this wave of sadness and the next thing I know I’m crying over a diaper commercial.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt low, but I’ve never wanted to hurt myself. My baby needs me, and I want to be here for her.

You've shared how the joy you once felt has slipped away since your baby arrived: laughter feels forced, plans feel like chores, and a constant gray cloud of sadness hangs over you. Most mornings start heavy, and even simple tasks-folding laundry, feeding yourself-feel overwhelming. You blame yourself whenever your daughter fusses, worry nonstop about her safety, and sometimes your heart races out of nowhere. Nights are restless; you lie awake cataloguing perceived mistakes or possible dangers, sleeping only in broken fragments. Yet through it all you've stayed determined to care for her and have never wished to harm yourself.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports almost no genuine laughter, describing forced chuckles that feel flat—closest to "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports complete loss of anticipatory pleasure—activities once enjoyed now feel obligatory and joyless, matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "pretty much every day" and provides vivid examples of persistent, intense guilt over normal infant crying, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-constant, intrusive, excessive worry about the baby's safety with compulsive checking, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete panic attacks occurring "a few times this week" without triggers, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm, inability to manage basic tasks, emotional collapse, and feeling barely able to cope, aligning with "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports nightly sleep disruption from intrusive thoughts, waking after brief sleep and lying awake for hours, totaling only ~4 broken hours nightly, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness present most of the time with only brief relief, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes (3-4×/week) tied to feeling overwhelmed and spontaneous sadness, aligning with "Yes, quite often."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** This score places you well above the ≥14 cutoff indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>. You endorse <sym>low mood</sym> most of the time, near-complete loss of interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), daily inappropriate guilt, prominent anxiety and panic-like episodes, middle and initial insomnia, tearfulness, and difficulty coping-meeting DSM-5 criteria thresholds. The severity and functional impact (self-care, infant care, partner support) warrant prompt evaluation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss treatment options
2. Ask about evidence-based therapies such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and consider <med>antidepressant medication</med> if recommended
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track progress
4. Enlist practical help overnight (partner, family, postpartum doula) so you can obtain four-hour stretches of sleep
5. Try 5-minute grounding exercises when panic surges: slow breathing, naming five things you can see
6. Limit Googling symptoms; instead call the pediatrician for reassurance about normal infant behaviors
7. Keep a simple log of mood, sleep, and crying spells to review with your provider
8. Contact <med>Postpartum Support International</med> (1-800-944-4773) for 24/7 support and local resources
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Screening Note – Postpartum Period (not a diagnostic assessment)

Presenting concerns endorsed by patient:
- Persistent low mood, “gray cloud,” frequent tearfulness
- Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment, activities feel obligatory)
- Daily self-blame/guilt, especially about infant care competence
- Continuous, intrusive worries regarding infant safety
- Two panic-like episodes (sudden racing heart, breathlessness, dread)
- Overwhelming fatigue and sense of being unable to “keep up”
- Mood-related insomnia (initial and middle; ~4 hrs interrupted/night)
- Crying spells 3–4×/week, sometimes provoked, sometimes spontaneous
- Denies any self-harm ideation

Consistent symptom pattern: low mood, anhedonia, guilt, and heightened anxiety co-occurring with functional impairment in infant care and self-care.

Risk indicators:
- EPDS-equivalent items: low pleasure, low mood, excessive self-blame, high anxiety, sleep disruption, frequent crying
- Safety: negative for suicidal or infanticidal thoughts at this time

Summary: Patient reports multiple symptoms consistent with postpartum depression/anxiety spectrum; intensity and chronicity warrant referral for comprehensive evaluation and possible treatment. No acute safety concerns identified today.
